analysis.one_liner: Caps price increases on essentials, hotels, rents, and repairs after a federally declared disaster.
analysis.headline: The bill to cap disaster price gouging was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee on March 27, 2025, and has seen no further action, with only one cosponsor.
analysis.plain_summary: After the president declares a major disaster or emergency, the bill would forbid sellers in the affected area from raising prices more than 10% above pre-disaster levels on essential goods and services, hotel rooms, and rents for 30 days, and on repair or reconstruction work for 180 days. It would also bar charging more than 50% above cost for 30 days. The FTC, state attorneys general, and private citizens could sue violators, and penalties collected by the FTC would go to help affected communities.
analysis.who_benefits: People in areas hit by federally declared disasters — including renters, hotel guests, and homeowners needing repairs — who would be protected from sudden price spikes on necessities during the recovery period. The bill's penalties would also fund aid to affected communities [S2, S3].

how_it_helps.text: Caps price increases for essential goods, hotel rooms, and rents at 10% above pre-disaster levels for 30 days, and repair/reconstruction services for 180 days [S2].
Bars sellers from charging more than 50% above their own cost for 30 days after a disaster declaration, targeting newly raised prices [S2].
Lets the FTC, state attorneys general, and individuals sue violators, with attorney's fees for winning plaintiffs and triple damages for willful violations [S3].
Directs civil penalties the FTC recovers into a fund to assist communities in the disaster area [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Sellers of essential goods, hotels, landlords, and repair contractors in disaster zones, who could face civil penalties up to $25,000 per violation (capped in total for related acts) and private lawsuits if they raise prices beyond the caps [S3].
analysis.who_pays_short: Sellers and landlords in disaster zones

drawbacks.text: The total civil penalty for related violations is capped at $25,000 per person (adjusted for inflation), a small amount for large chains, which weakens the deterrence the bill is meant to create [S3].

Price ceilings during shortages can cause goods to disappear from shelves if sellers cannot raise prices enough to cover sudden scarcity; the bill's cost-based exception mitigates but does not eliminate this risk, and honest supporters would acknowledge it [S3].

Private lawsuits are limited to actual monetary loss plus attorney's fees, with treble damages only at a court's discretion for willful violations, so recovery for individual consumers may be modest [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill addresses a real harm: disaster price spikes hit people at their most vulnerable, and state gouging laws are patchy. The cap on rent and lodging increases could create temporary shortages or deter suppliers from rushing goods into a disaster zone, though the cost-based exception is designed to let prices rise enough to cover genuine supply costs. The modest penalty cap limits how much the federal enforcement would deter large chains, a real design weakness. On balance, for people in disaster areas the protection would likely outweigh those costs, but the bill never advanced far enough to be tested.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the House Energy and Commerce Committee, which never acted on it, so no committee or floor vote has taken place.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on March 27, 2025 and referred the same day to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce [S1].
The full action history shows no further steps: no hearings, no markup, no committee vote, and no floor action [S5].
It attracted only one cosponsor, a House Democrat, in addition to its sponsor [S4].
As written, the bill would treat disaster price gouging as an unfair practice the FTC can penalize, and would let states and private citizens sue violators [S3].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No outcome has occurred yet. If the bill remains stalled, hotels, landlords, retailers, and repair firms that raise prices sharply after disasters are better off because the caps never take effect.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: No outcome yet; bill still pending

for.name: Rep. Laura Friedman
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and became its lead sponsor.

for.name: Rep. Brad Sherman
for.what_they_did: Joined as an original cosponsor at introduction.

for.name: House Committee on Energy and Commerce
for.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and has taken no action on it — no hearing, markup, or vote has been scheduled.

sides.party_line_note: Both sponsors are Democrats and no Republicans have signed on, but the bill never reached a vote, so no one has had to take a recorded position for or against it [S4].

industries.industry: Hotels, landlords, and retailers of essential goods in disaster zones
industries.note: The bill bars them from raising rents, lodging rates, and prices for essentials by more than 10% after a disaster, and caps markup at 50% above cost. It would end the practice of charging stranded families premium prices exactly when they cannot shop around.
Repair and reconstruction prices would be capped for 180 days, the longest window in the bill, directly limiting post-disaster contractor pricing.

analysis.trajectory: With a single cosponsor, no committee action in months, and no indication the Energy and Commerce Committee will schedule a hearing or markup, the bill is very likely to sit without action for the rest of the 119th Congress, as most House bills that never receive a committee markup do.
